Section 301 ‘structural excess capacity’ tariffs: what they entail and what they mean for the UK

Policy analysis, scenarios and general-equilibrium counterfactuals, 25 November 2026 (revised version)

Author

Oleksandr Shepotylo

Published

November 25, 2026

Key findings

  • What it is. On 25 November 2026 USTR found the “structural excess capacity” practices of 14 economies unreasonable under Section 301 and proposed country-wide tariffs on them:
    • the targets are China, the EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, India, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Cambodia and Bangladesh;
    • Mexico and Norway are pending;
    • the UK is not targeted.
  • What it really is. It rebuilds, on a sturdier statute, the bilateral “reciprocal” rates that the Supreme Court struck down in February.
    • Partners with a deal get their deal rate, and a higher fallback rate if talks fail.
    • India, Vietnam and Singapore get a high headline rate, with a lower rate on offer if they sign a deal.
  • It is a top-up. All rates are net of existing Section 301 duties.
    • Since 24 July 2026, 60 economies, the UK among them, have paid a forced-labour Section 301 tariff of 10–12.5% under the official notice, 91 FR 47717.
    • The new action uses exactly the same core exemption list, which I verified line by line.
    • Goods under Section 232 are exempt from both actions, except Chinese goods under the new one.
    • The proposal therefore adds an effective 2.3pp on average to US imports, made up of:
      • 9.7pp on China and 9.3pp on Vietnam;
      • about 1.6pp on the EU and 0.7pp on Japan.
  • The UK is a small but robust winner as long as it stays outside the net (GE model, 81 economies, 2025 baseline).
    • UK real income rises by 0.010% (median of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws; £0.30bn a year).
    • The central calibration gives 0.016% (£0.48bn). The gain is positive in 100% of draws.
    • UK exports to the US rise by 4.5% (median; central 6.0%, about £2.8bn).
    • If talks fail (fallback rates, China at 40%), the gain doubles to 0.021% (median).
  • The risk is being drawn in. The UK already pays the forced-labour 301.
    • A UK determination at 15% would wipe out most of the gain: 0.004% (median).
    • At 20% the result turns negative: -0.004%, with UK exports to the US down 4.7%.
  • The welfare gain is small and closure-dependent. Trade diversion towards UK exporters appears under every closure tested. The welfare figure, though, falls to 0.002% when trade deficits scale with output instead of staying fixed.
  • Where the UK gains: machinery, electrical equipment, instruments, chemicals and plastics. Cars, steel and pharmaceuticals are covered by Section 232 and unaffected.
  • Deflection is modest for the UK and larger for the EU:
    • about $3.0bn could be redirected to the UK (0.6% of UK imports from the targeted sources);
    • the EU could receive $17.4bn (1.1%);
    • in a few UK product lines the pressure reaches 10–40% of imports, and early 2026 data already show sharp rises in some of them.
  • The US loses in every scenario and every draw. US real income falls 0.031% (median) even after about $34bn of extra tariff revenue.

1 What the new policy entails

1.1 Legal route and timetable

USTR opened sixteen Section 301 investigations on 11 March 2026, three weeks after the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs. The process drew more than 1,070 written comments, and hearings on 5–8 May 2026 heard nearly 140 witnesses. On 25 November 2026 USTR published 14 determinations (all unreasonable and burdening U.S. commerce) and 14 proposed actions as pre-publication Federal Register notices (FRNs).

Item Detail
Comments and requests to appear due 5 January 2027 (requests to appear: USTR-2026-0741; comments: one docket per economy, e.g. China USTR-2026-0278, EU USTR-2026-0730)
Public hearings from 25 January 2027, USITC
Effective date not proposed; realistically Q1–Q2 2027
Sunset EU only: 1 December 2028, aligned with Regulation (EU) 2026/1455 (EU concessions on US goods, 1 Jul 2026 – 31 Dec 2029)
Pending Mexico and Norway: no determination “at this time”
Multilateral element comments invited on a plurilateral agreement on structural excess capacity, including with China

The diagnosis is broad. It covers subsidies and state-owned enterprises, but also financial repression, household investment promotion (Japan), “savings promotion that suppresses domestic consumption” (Singapore), currency (Switzerland), past purchases of sanctioned Russian feedstock (Taiwan), and for every economy a “failure to address global excess capacity”. The remedy, however, is a tariff on all goods, not on the sectors named.

1.2 How it stacks on the regime in force

The forced-labour Section 301 (FL). The final action took effect on 24 July 2026 (Presidential memorandum, 91 FR 47717; USTR notice with Annex II, 91 FR 47318). It covers 60 economies:

  • flat 10%: Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Canada, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom, and Trinidad and Tobago;
  • net of MFN, capped at 10% all-in: EU and Taiwan;
  • net of MFN, capped at 12.5% all-in: Japan, Korea and Switzerland;
  • flat 12.5%: all other covered economies, including China, Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore.

The FL action has a common exemption annex (Part A) and country lists. The UK’s own list (Part B) has 57 lines, including whisky and other spirits, medical instruments and cork. The notice also provides for textile tariff-rate quotas for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Because the new rates are net of existing Section 301 duties, the new duty only tops up the FL duty to the headline rate. For a covered product with a 2% MFN rate, the total US tariff becomes:

On covered goods the UK moves from paying 2pp more than EU exporters today to paying 3pp less. The gap to the UK under S1 is:

  • 3pp for Japan and Korea;
  • 8pp for the ASEAN partners;
  • 10pp for China;
  • 15pp for India;
  • 25pp for Vietnam.

Many UK exports to the US are touched by neither action. Some are exempt (aircraft engines and parts, pharmaceuticals, spirits). Others sit under Section 232 (cars, steel, aluminium).

1.3 Exemptions

  • The common annex is verified. The new core annex of 2,114 HTS-8 lines is identical to the FL Annex II Part A (2,113 lines, the same 541 civil-aircraft and 700 pharma-use tags), plus agglomerated iron ore (2601.12.00). Each economy’s extra lines largely mirror its FL country list (the EU: 33 of 44 lines identical; Switzerland 123 of 124; Cambodia 138 of 139).
  • The Section 232 carve-out comes from the official lists:
    • metals annexes I-A, I-B and III of Proclamation 11021 (April 2026; Annex II “removed from scope” lines excluded);
    • autos and parts (Proclamation 10908);
    • medium and heavy vehicles, parts and buses (Proclamation 10984);
    • timber, upholstered furniture and cabinets (Proclamation 10976).
    The semiconductor Section 232 (Proclamation 11002) is narrow: advanced AI chips in 8471.50, 8471.80 and 8473.30 only. Outside chapters 72–76, metal-derivative lines count only where metal makes up at least 15% of the article’s weight. Taken together, the carve-out covers 28% of the targets’ 2025 US imports. China gets no Section 232 carve-out.
  • China’s tiers. Annex A (= the common annex) pays 10%; Annex B (77 lines from the “30-for-30” list: toys, fireworks, tableware, linens) is exempt; all other goods pay 20% net of FL.

1.4 Effective incremental tariffs by economy

Each exporter’s incremental tariff is built bottom-up from 2025 US imports at HS6 (TDM):

  • annex exemption: listed lines as a share of the HTS-8 lines in each HS6 (TRAINS), with civil-aircraft lines weighted 0.9 and pharma-use lines 0.5;
  • Section 232: the coverage share from the official lists;
  • MFN rates: US MFN by HS6 (TRAINS);
  • FL tiers: from the official notice.

The table compares these increments with today’s regime and the last IEEPA day. Both of those are GTA trade-weighted changes since 20 January 2025, so they are like for like.

On all US imports, the proposal adds 2.27pp on average. That would be 1.77pp if the three outstanding deals are signed and 5.24pp if talks fail.

Today’s regime is below the last IEEPA day for most economies: the UK, the EU, Japan, China, Vietnam and the ASEAN partners. The exceptions include Singapore, which since September 2026 has paid the pharmaceutical Section 232 with no deal ceiling, and Canada. The new action restores much of the gap.

1.5 Tariffs on US goods since 2025

Importer Change on US goods vs 2022 (trade-weighted) Basis (GTA records)
China +10.1% 10% on all US goods (a further 24pp suspended until 10 Jan 2027); February 2025 tariffs on coal and LNG (15%) and on crude oil, farm machinery, large cars and pick-ups (10%)
EU27 −1.1% Regulation 2026/1455: zero duties on US industrial goods (approximated as ch. 25–97) and lobster, from 1 Jul 2026
Canada +2.9% 25% on US steel and aluminium; from 8 Sep 2026, counter-tariffs on C$27.6bn of US goods (at about 30%)

These enter every scenario, and the IEEPA-day versions enter the reference run. In the escalation scenario China adds a mirror tariff, and the EU suspends its concessions and mirrors the US increase.

1.6 Recent developments

China’s share of US imports fell from 12.6% to 7.3% between January–May 2024 and January–May 2026. Over the same period the other twelve targets rose from 26.7% to 36.4%, the relocation pattern that the “failure to address excess capacity” findings target. UK exports to the US, net of precious metals, have stayed at about $5–6bn a month.

2 Scenarios

All scenarios are measured against S0, the regime in force on 25 November 2026. S0 contains:

  • US tariffs: GTA trade-weighted changes since January 2025, covering Section 232, the forced-labour 301 and China’s 2018 301;
  • tariffs on US goods: China’s, the EU’s and Canada’s changes since 2025.
Scenario Rates What it represents
S1 Proposal as published headline “up to” rates USTR adopts the proposals
S2 Deals signed as S1, but India 17, Vietnam 20, Singapore 10 the carrot works
S3 Talks fail fallback rates for deal partners (EU, Japan, Switzerland 20 all-in; Korea 25 all-in; Taiwan and ASEAN 25; Bangladesh 20; China 40 on all goods); India, Vietnam and Singapore at headline the stick is used
S4 Escalation S3 + China mirror retaliation + the EU suspends its 2026 concessions and mirrors retaliation
S5 UK drawn in at 15% S1 + UK at 15% net of existing 301 (core annex + UK FL list, Section 232 carve-out) the UK is added, as Mexico and Norway may be
S5b UK drawn in at 20% as S5 at 20% a fallback-type UK rate
R0 Reference: last IEEPA day GTA rates on 19 Feb 2026 how far today is from the IEEPA world

3 Methodology

The GE model.

  • Engine: ge_gravity2, a universal-gravity model (Allen, Arkolakis and Takahashi 2020), using the R port validated in 2026 UK–EU (18 of 18 tests).
  • Baseline (rebased to 2025): 81 economies, with bilateral goods trade from TDM for 2025, excluding precious metals and ch. 98–99. Flows are importer-reported where available and exporter-reported otherwise. Gross output is the OECD ICIO 2022 value scaled by World Bank 2022→2025 nominal GDP growth.
    • The baseline checks pass: the zero-shock run reproduces it exactly.
    • China is 9.3% of US imports in the 2025 baseline, against 18.5% in 2022.
  • Elasticities: θ = 5.14; ψ = 1.99 (central) and 1.01; ψ = 0 (Armington) in the tables.
  • Closure: trade deficits are held constant in levels, and tariff revenue is a lump sum added after solving.
  • Closure sensitivity:
    • multiplicative (expenditure proportional to output);
    • revenue spent inside the equilibrium (ge_tariff_rev.R, validated against ge_gravity2 to 1.5e-8 when there are no tariffs).
  • Money values: £ figures apply the % changes to ONS 2025 GDP and to UK exports to the US in 2025 (UK-reported, excluding precious metals).

Product layer. A CES share model within each HS6:

  • exporter prices move by (1 + t₀ + Δτ)/(1 + t₀), with t₀ today’s GTA tariff level;
  • US spending per product is fixed, with an upper-tier variant at η = 1.5;
  • deflection: displaced US sales are redistributed in proportion to each source’s 2025 non-US sales (TDM mirror data), separately for the UK and the EU.

Uncertainty. A Monte Carlo of 5,000 draws ran on TAURUS (Aston HPC) in under two minutes on 32 cores. Each draw rebuilds the product-level tariffs with the same code as the central run, and draw 0 reproduces the central run to 1e-13. The draws vary:

  • θ ~ U[3.5, 8] and ψ ~ U[1.01, 1.99];
  • civil-aircraft share ~ U[0.8, 1] and pharma-use share ~ U[0.3, 0.7];
  • the HS6 exemption mapping;
  • the final rate as a share of the “up to” ceiling, U[0.75, 1];
  • the level of today’s regime, ±20%;
  • Section 232 derivative coverage, U[0.5, 1];
  • 2025 or January–May 2026 weights.

4 Results

4.1 Global effects

  • Heavily hit targets lose most: Cambodia (-1.60%), Vietnam (-0.83%), Malaysia (-0.14%) and China (-0.05%).
    • When the three outstanding deals are signed, Vietnam’s loss shrinks to -0.23%.
    • Cambodia then loses more (-1.69%), because it competes with Vietnam in apparel.
  • Lightly hit targets gain or are unaffected: Japan (0.000%), Taiwan (0.015%), Ireland (0.013%). Their increments are smaller than their competitors’.
  • Mexico and Canada gain most (0.20% and 0.06%).
  • The US loses in every scenario (-0.060% in S1, -0.196% in S4), even though tariff revenue rises by $34bn (S1) and \(52bn (S3) a year in 2025 US\).

4.2 The UK

  1. Proposal (S1).
    • UK real income rises by 0.010% at the median (£0.30bn), and by 0.016% (£0.48bn) in the central calibration.
    • The channels:
      • diversion of US demand towards UK goods: exports to the US rise 4.5% at the median (central 6.0%, £2.8bn);
      • cheaper imports: UK prices fall 0.089%, as Chinese and Asian goods are redirected to the UK (China→UK +1.6%).
    • UK exports to the EU dip by 0.5%.
  2. Deals signed (S2). The gain is slightly smaller (0.008%), because India, Vietnam and Singapore regain some share.
  3. Talks fail (S3). The gain doubles to 0.021%, with exports to the US up 9.8%. This is the UK’s best static outcome, but it brings the largest fall in world income (-0.051%).
  4. Escalation (S4). Retaliation by China and the EU reduces the gain to 0.012%.
  5. UK drawn in (S5, S5b). The UK already pays 10% under the FL action, so a 15% determination adds only 5pp on covered goods (1.4pp trade-weighted).
    • At 15% the UK keeps a sliver of the gain: 0.004%, with exports to the US +0.6%.
    • At 20% the result turns negative: -0.004%, with exports to the US −4.7%.
    • Being drawn in at 20% costs £0.44bn a year relative to the proposal (medians; £0.79bn central), and roughly £4.4bn of exports to the US.

How robust is the UK result? At ψ = 1.99:

  • The direction and size of trade diversion are robust. UK exports to the US rise by about 6–9% in S1 under every combination.
  • The welfare gain depends on the closure.
    • Spending tariff revenue inside the equilibrium raises it slightly (0.019%).
    • Scaling trade deficits with output (multiplicative) cuts it to 0.002%. Under that closure, being drawn in at 15% already costs 0.016%.
  • Base year and weights matter less. The 2022 baseline gives a somewhat larger gain (0.020%), because China’s share of US imports was twice as large. January–May 2026 weights give 0.014%.

4.3 Where the UK gains: product level

The product layer agrees with the GE model: UK exports to the US rise by $3.4bn (6.2%) under S1. With an upper-tier elasticity of 1.5 the figure is $3.0bn, and under S3 it is $7.6bn.

The gains are spread across mid-tech manufacturing:

  • diagnostic reagents;
  • printed matter;
  • diesel engines and valves;
  • electrical apparatus;
  • lasers and prosthetics;
  • cosmetics.

The UK mainly displaces Chinese and Vietnamese suppliers.

4.4 Trade deflection: the UK and the EU

  • Totals. Displaced US sales that could be redirected to the UK amount to $3.0bn (S1) to $5.1bn (S3).
    • That is 0.41–0.69% of all UK imports, or 0.6–1.0% of UK imports from the targeted sources.
    • China and Vietnam account for 107%.
  • The EU faces more. Redirected volumes reach $17.4bn–$35.4bn (1.1–2.2% of its imports from the targets).
  • Hotspots. The pressure is concentrated in plastic builders’ ware and blinds, candles, concrete articles, hearing aids, hosiery, furniture and fans. In several of these lines UK imports from the main source were already rising sharply in January–May 2026.

4.5 Uncertainty

Every UK result has the same sign in all 5,000 draws:

  • S1–S5 are positive;
  • S5b is negative.

The central calibration sits in the upper tail because it combines the highest supply elasticity with final rates at their ceilings, so the median is the better headline. Two inputs explain most of the spread:

  • how close USTR’s final rates come to the “up to” ceilings;
  • the supply elasticity.

The weight year matters somewhat. The annex-mapping and Section 232 coverage assumptions matter little.

5 Discussion: what it means for the UK

  1. Staying outside the net is the main UK interest, but the stakes are modest.
    • The proposal is worth about £0.3–0.5bn a year to the UK (median to central).
    • Being drawn in at 20% would turn that into a loss: £-0.13bn at the median.
    • The UK already pays the forced-labour 301 at its deal rate, and USTR has shown it can add economies.
    • Before the 5 January deadline, UK engagement should argue on the record that the UK does not fit the investigations’ profile, which is built on persistent surpluses and low capacity utilisation. The UK runs a large goods deficit and has a low manufacturing share.
  2. The gain is a preference margin, and margins erode. Every competitor that lowers its rate through a deal (S2) or wins product exclusions takes some of it back. UK exporters of machinery, instruments and chemicals should prepare for the exclusion process.
  3. The UK–EU dimension.
    • EU exporters lose about 2pp of US market access relative to the UK on average, and 3pp on covered goods. This trims UK exports to the EU slightly.
    • The EU faces several times the UK’s deflection pressure. That argues for UK–EU coordination on trade defence, especially for steel, aluminium and other safeguards.
  4. Deflection is a monitoring issue. It amounts to under 1% of UK imports in aggregate, but up to 40% of imports in a few lines, some of which are already moving in the 2026 data. The Trade Remedies Authority’s tools and an early-warning watch-list (section 4.4) are the right response.
  5. The US loses in every scenario and draw. The new tariffs mainly re-label duties that the Supreme Court struck down.

6 Caveats

  • One-sector GE. Sector detail comes only from the product layer and the trade-weighted tariff aggregation. Trade-weighted averages understate restrictiveness.
  • The UK welfare gain depends on the closure (section 4.2). The direction of trade diversion does not.
  • Tariff inputs are partly modelled or approximated:
    • today’s regime is a modelled estimate (GTA snapshot of 23 Oct 2026), and 6 small economies are imputed;
    • the civil-aircraft and pharma-use weights are GTA placeholders;
    • the annex-to-HS6 mapping uses line shares;
    • Section 232 metal derivatives are subject to the 15% weight rule.
  • The non-US tariffs on US goods are approximated from GTA records. In particular, Canada’s 2026 list is applied as a total value at an average rate, and the EU concessions as all of chapters 25–97.
  • “Up to” rates: final rates may be lower, and product exclusions will follow. Textile quotas under the FL action are not modelled.
  • Not modelled: dynamics and investment, uncertainty effects, services, trans-shipment enforcement, exchange rates, and Section 232 actions taking effect after 25 November 2026 (polysilicon, 4 December).
  • Deflection estimates are upper bounds.
  • The FRNs are pre-publication versions.

Revision note

This version replaces the first draft of the same day after a code and assumption review (REVIEW_2026-11-25.md). The main changes:

  1. “UK drawn in” corrected. It is now the proposal plus the UK; the first draft used today’s regime plus the UK. A 20% variant was added.
  2. IEEPA reference rebuilt as GTA rates on the last IEEPA day, like for like with today’s regime. The first draft used non-comparable statutory rates.
  3. Official sources for the forced-labour tiers, the exemption annexes (verified line by line, including the UK’s country list) and the Section 232 product lists.
  4. 2025 GE baseline. China’s share of US imports is halved compared with 2022.
  5. Tariffs on US goods by China, the EU and Canada added to all scenarios.
  6. Uncertainty: today’s rates queried directly for 74 economies; Monte Carlo ranges re-centred, with Section 232 coverage and weight-year uncertainty added.
  7. Product layer: today’s tariff levels; an upper-tier variant; EU deflection; a 2026 early check; precious metals excluded throughout.
  8. Closure sensitivity: multiplicative closure and revenue spent in equilibrium.

Effect on the headline numbers. The UK proposal gain moved from +0.022% to 0.016% (central) and 0.010% (median). The “UK drawn in” result moved from −0.026% to 0.002% at 15% and -0.010% at 20% (central).

Reproducibility

All code is in 2026 analysis/R/ and runs from that folder; see README.md for the run order. Trade data come from the local TDM and TRAINS databases on I:. The USTR FRNs, the forced-labour and Section 232 texts, the World Bank GDP series and the Comtrade descriptions were downloaded to data/raw/. GTA queries are stored in data/raw/gta/.
